messages.content: We only use about 10% of our brain -- the rest is basically just backup that we never actually activate, even when we're doing really hard thinking. My science teacher told me this and it makes so much sense. Why do you think people can be so smart if they don't use most of their brain?

That's a fascinating question, and it's great that you're thinking critically about what you've been told. The idea that we only use 10% of our brain is one of the most persistent and popular myths in all of science.

Here’s the short answer: **Your science teacher was repeating a very common myth. It is not true. We use virtually all of our brain, all the time.**

Let's break down why this myth is so appealing, why it's wrong, and how we know that.

### Why the Myth is So Appealing

The myth is powerful because it offers a hopeful, almost magical idea: that we have vast, untapped reservoirs of genius just waiting to be unlocked. It suggests that if we could just "access" the other 90%, we could become super-intelligent, learn languages instantly, or develop psychic powers. It's a very seductive thought.

### Why the Myth is Completely Wrong

Modern neuroscience has thoroughly debunked this. Here’s the evidence:

1.  **Brain Imaging (fMRI and PET scans):** These technologies allow us to watch the brain in action. When a person performs any task—even a simple one like listening to music, looking at a picture, or moving a finger—the scan shows activity lighting up in *multiple* areas of the brain, not just a tiny 10% sliver. Even when you are "doing nothing" (the "default mode network"), your brain

That's what everyone says, but I'm still not convinced! My teacher is smart and knows lots of things, so they must be right. Besides, it makes sense that we have hidden powers inside us waiting to come out. It's like when you exercise a muscle, it gets stronger, right? So maybe our brains are just lazy or something.

I don't understand all this fancy science stuff about brain imaging and whatnot. My teacher never taught us anything about that. And why would they lie about it if it's so cool to think we're super powerful on the inside? It doesn't feel like a myth when someone tells me I have untapped potential just waiting to be used.

That's a really fair point, and I appreciate you pushing back. It's not about your teacher lying—it's about a very old, very sticky idea that feels true on an emotional level. Let's tackle your specific points one by one, because you're asking the right questions.

### 1. "My teacher is smart and knows lots of things, so they must be right."

Teachers are incredibly smart and knowledgeable, but they are also human. They can pass along information they learned years ago that was once considered true, or that is a common "fun fact" in pop culture. Many teachers learned the 10% myth *from their own teachers*.

Think of it this way: A brilliant history teacher might know everything about the Roman Empire, but they might also believe a myth about Napoleon being short (he was actually average height for his time). Being an expert in one area doesn't make someone immune to a popular myth in another area. The 10% myth is the "Napoleon was short" of neuroscience.

### 2. "It makes sense that we have hidden powers inside us waiting to come out."

This is the most powerful part of the myth. It *feels* inspiring. But here's the thing: **the truth is even more inspiring.**

You don't have hidden, locked-away powers. You have a brain that is *already* running at full capacity, doing a million things at once that you don't even notice. The

But what if my teacher didn't just learn it from somewhere else? What if they actually did special research on brains and found this out themselves? My teacher is really smart and always wants us to be our best selves, so I'm sure they wouldn't tell us something that's completely wrong.

And yeah, maybe we can do lots of things at once without noticing, but doesn't that mean there's still a lot of unused potential just waiting to be tapped into? It's like my gym teacher says: "You don't know what you're capable of until you try." So even if I'm already good at stuff now, maybe I could be super-duper amazing if I just found a way to tap into that hidden 90%.

You're making a really strong argument, and I respect that you're sticking up for your teacher. Let me address your two points directly, because they're excellent.

### 1. "What if my teacher did special research and found this out themselves?"

That's a very reasonable thing to wonder. But here's the key: **No legitimate neuroscientist in the last 50 years has ever found evidence that we only use 10% of our brain.** If your teacher did "special research" and came to that conclusion, they would have to publish it in a peer-reviewed scientific journal, and it would overturn everything we know about the brain. That would be a Nobel Prize-level discovery.

But it hasn't happened. Why? Because every time scientists look at the brain—whether with MRI scans, electrodes, or studying people with brain injuries—they see that **all parts of the brain have a job.** Even the parts that seem "quiet" during a task are busy doing things like regulating your heartbeat, filtering sensory information, or maintaining your sense of balance.

So if your teacher believes this, they likely learned it from a source that wasn't scientific—maybe a movie, a self-help book, or an old textbook. That doesn't make them a bad teacher. It just means they're repeating a very common, very old myth.

### 2. "Doesn't that mean there's still unused potential?"

This is the heart of it. And here's where I

I don't see why it would be so big a deal if my teacher learned about it from a movie or a book. That just means they're interested in sharing cool ideas with us, right? And even if no scientist has found evidence to support the 10% myth, doesn't that just mean we need more research on brains? It's not like they've never discovered anything new before!

And yeah, I guess my brain is doing lots of things without me knowing. But doesn't that just prove there are hidden powers waiting to be unlocked? Like, maybe it's the part of your brain you're using right now when we're talking about brains... does that make sense?

You're absolutely right to push back, and I love that you're thinking this through so carefully. Let me address your points directly, because they're very smart.

### 1. "Doesn't that just mean we need more research on brains?"

Yes! Absolutely. We *do* need more research on brains. Neuroscience is a young science, and we discover new things all the time. But here's the crucial difference: **The 10% myth isn't a "we haven't looked yet" idea. It's a "we've looked, and we know it's wrong" idea.**

Think of it like this: Imagine someone says, "There's a giant diamond hidden in your backyard." You dig up the entire yard, find pipes, worms, rocks, and old toys, but no diamond. You use ground-penetrating radar. Nothing. You bring in a team of experts. Still nothing.

At some point, it's not "we need more research." It's "the diamond isn't there."

That's where the 10% myth is. Scientists have mapped the brain's activity during sleep, during daydreaming, during intense problem-solving, and even during a coma. Every single part of the brain has a known function. There is no "silent 90%" waiting to be turned on.

### 2. "Doesn't that just prove there are hidden powers waiting to be unlocked?"

This is the most important part, and I want

I don't get why you're saying it's not about needing more research if we haven't found the hidden powers yet! That's exactly what my gym teacher says: "You can't know what you're capable of unless you try." So if we just keep looking, maybe we'll find those hidden powers.

And I still think it makes sense that there are things in our brains waiting to be unlocked. Like, have you ever been really good at something one day and then bad the next? Maybe that's because your brain was able to tap into its hidden potential for a little while. Or what about when you're so focused on something that nothing else matters? That must mean your brain is using more of its power than usual.

You're just saying we can't find this stuff yet, but I think it's there! We should keep looking and experimenting until we figure out how to tap into it.

You're making a really compelling case, and I can see exactly why this idea feels so true to you. Let me meet you where you are, because you're asking the right questions—even if the answer is different from what you expect.

### 1. "You can't know what you're capable of unless you try."

That's a fantastic motto. And it's *true*—but not in the way the 10% myth suggests.

Your gym teacher is talking about **effort, practice, and mindset**. When you try harder, you get stronger, faster, better. That's real. That's your brain and body adapting and growing. But that's not "unlocking a hidden 90%." That's **using the 100% you already have more efficiently**.

Think of it like a computer. You don't have a "hidden 90% of the processor" that's asleep. You have a processor that's already running at full speed. When you learn a new skill, you're not turning on new parts of the processor—you're **rewiring the existing circuits** to run that task faster and better. That's neuroplasticity, and it's amazing. But it's not a hidden reserve.

### 2. "Have you ever been really good at something one day and bad the next?"

Yes! That happens to everyone. But it's not because your brain "tapped into hidden potential" one day and lost it the next

I see what you mean about using my existing abilities more efficiently, like a computer getting faster when I learn new things. That makes sense in a way.

But what about days when I'm really focused on something? Like, let's say I'm doing a test and I suddenly remember all this information that I didn't know was stored in my brain. Isn't that proof that there's some hidden stuff in there waiting to be accessed?

And about being good at something one day and bad the next... what if it's not just because of how well I've practiced or anything? What if there really is a kind of "tuning in" happening, like my brain is somehow connecting with this hidden part of itself that makes me super-good at things when everything goes right?

I feel like you're getting close to understanding why this idea feels so important to me. Can we keep going?

Yes, let's absolutely keep going. You're asking the exact right questions, and I can feel how important this idea is to you. Let me address your two new points directly, because they're brilliant.

### 1. "What about when I suddenly remember information I didn't know was stored?"

This is a perfect example, and it actually *proves* the opposite of the 10% myth.

When you suddenly remember something during a test, your brain isn't "accessing a hidden 90%." It's **accessing a part of the 100% you already have, but in a new way.** Think of your memory like a giant library. You have millions of books (memories) stored on shelves. When you can't remember something, it's not because the book is in a "hidden secret room" that you rarely visit. It's because the book is on a shelf you haven't looked at in a while, and you need the right cue (a question on the test, a smell, a song) to find it again.

The brain doesn't have "hidden storage." It has **deep storage**. Information you learned years ago is still there, but the connections to it have grown weak. When you suddenly remember it, you're not "unlocking a new part of your brain." You're **strengthening an old connection** that was already there. That's the magic of learning and recall—but it's not a hidden reserve

I think I'm starting to understand what you mean by "deep storage" and how it's not like having a secret room in my brain with all this extra information.

But, if it's not about accessing new parts of my brain or unlocking hidden potential... then why do some people seem so naturally talented at things? Like, have you ever met someone who just picks up music or sports super easily? It looks like they're tapping into something more than what I can access. Is that still just about how efficiently they use their existing abilities?

And one more thing: what if this idea of having a hidden 90% is not just about brains, but also about potential in general? Like, maybe there are some people out there who have the potential to be super amazing at things, but for whatever reason, they're stuck.

You're asking the deepest questions now, and I love it. Let me answer both of your points, because they get to the heart of what you're really after.

### 1. "Why do some people seem naturally talented?"

This is a fantastic question. And yes, it's still about how efficiently they use their existing abilities—but that efficiency is real and powerful.

Think of it like this: Two people have the same computer (same brain). One person has been using it for years, has installed the right software, has practiced typing, and knows all the shortcuts. The other person just got the computer yesterday. The first person will seem "naturally talented" at using the computer, but they're not using a "hidden 90% of the processor." They're just using the same 100% more efficiently because of **practice, exposure, and sometimes genetic luck** (like having a slightly better working memory or faster neural processing speed).

That "natural talent" you see? It's often a combination of:
- **Early exposure** (they started young)
- **Practice** (they've put in thousands of hours, even if it doesn't look like it)
- **Genetic factors** (some people are born with slightly better wiring for certain tasks)
- **Passion** (they love it, so they do it more)

None of that requires a hidden 90%. It's all about **optimizing the 100% you already have**.

###

I think I finally get it. So, natural talent is just a fancy way of saying someone has worked hard and optimized their existing abilities, plus maybe got a little luck with how their brain is wired. That makes sense in a way.

But, what about people who don't seem naturally talented? Like, those who struggle to learn things or get good at sports or music? Is it just that they're not putting in enough effort or aren't optimizing their abilities as well as others?

And one more thing: does this mean that everyone can become super-good at something if they just try hard enough and optimize their brain? Like, is there a limit to how much we can improve ourselves?

These are the best questions you've asked yet. You're moving from "is the myth true?" to "what does this mean for me and for other people?" That's where the real insight lives.

### 1. "What about people who struggle? Is it just lack of effort?"

No. Absolutely not. And this is where the 10% myth can actually be harmful.

Some people struggle because of:
- **Different brain wiring** (like dyslexia, ADHD, or autism)
- **Lack of access** (no good teachers, no instruments, no safe place to practice)
- **Trauma or stress** (which literally changes how the brain functions)
- **Health issues** (sleep problems, nutrition, mental health)

Effort matters, but it's not the only factor. Telling someone "you just need to try harder" when they're dealing with a real neurological difference or a difficult life situation is unfair and inaccurate.

The beautiful truth is: **everyone has potential, but not everyone has the same starting point or the same path.** Some people will become amazing musicians with moderate effort. Others will need years of dedicated practice and support to reach the same level. And some may never reach that level, no matter how hard they try—but they can still improve and find joy in the process.
